To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The brain is protected by the blood-brain barrier, which is a complex system that regulates transport of drugs into and from the central nervous system.

(i) the BBB can be a barrier for drug entry into the CNS, (ii) the BBB can also act as a gatekeeper for the brain by regulating drug entry into the brain parenchyma, (iii) drug efflux transporters are important for drug disposition in the brain, (iv) drug efflux transporter activity is regulated by drug exposure and disease state, (v) the BBB is a complex structure with multiple functions, which should be considered in drug development.

the blood–brain barrier (BBB) is an important factor in the development of central nervous system (CNS) drugs, but that too much attention has been paid to permeability and too few studies have focused on transport, the limiting factor in drug penetration.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel and integrated approach to the discovery, design, and development of drugs for the brain.
the transport of drugs across the blood brain barrier (BBB), and the effect of this transport on the pharmacokinetics of the drugs in the central nervous system (CNS).

the development of a novel and integrated approach for the development of new CNS drugs, based on the use of in vitro models and in silico models for the prediction of BBB drug permeability and drug-drug interactions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the BBB is not the major problem in drug delivery to brain, but that the major problem lies in the transport processes of the BBB.
the current understanding of BBB transport and its impact on the CNS effects of drugs is insufficient to support a rational design of CNS drugs.
the BBB is not a barrier to drug delivery to the CNS, but that it is a transport barrier that can be overcome by the use of appropriate drug delivery methods.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is a need for a more integrated approach to drug discovery and development.
the brain is a complex and dynamic organ that is not easily accessible.
the BBB is not the only obstacle to brain delivery of drugs, and the BBB is not a barrier for all compounds.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the BBB can be a major barrier to the development of CNS drugs, but it can also be an important target for the design and optimization of CNS drugs.
a better understanding of the BBB transport and the CNS effects of drugs is needed to improve the translation of drug development.

it is important to collect pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic information in the preclinical setting and that it is necessary to understand how the BBB transports the drug and what effects the BBB transport has on pharmacokinetic parameters.
